title: Bottling and closures
subtitle: The last steps
objectives: Explain why wine is clarified and stabilised
Compare cork, screw cap and other closures
Explain the effect of the closure on ageing

steps.title: Clarifying and stabilising
steps.body: Before bottling, wine is made clear and stable. Fining adds an agent like bentonite clay or egg white that binds haze-causing particles. Filtration strains them out. Cold stabilisation chills the wine to drop tartrate crystals, the harmless wine diamonds sometimes found in bottles. Some producers skip these steps, accepting a little haze.

steps.title: Closures and oxygen
steps.body: Natural cork lets in tiny amounts of oxygen, but about 1 to 3% of bottles can be tainted by TCA, which smells of damp cardboard. Screw caps let in very little oxygen and cannot cause cork taint, so they keep fruit fresh; they are standard in New Zealand and Australia. Technical corks and glass stoppers sit in between.
steps.highlight: Cork breathes a little; screw caps barely at all

steps.prompt: What are the crystals sometimes found in a bottle of white wine?
steps.explanation: Tartrates are natural salts of tartaric acid. They are harmless and show the wine wasn't cold stabilised.

steps.body: A screw cap isn't a sign of a cheap wine. Many top Rieslings, Sauvignon Blancs and even fine reds use them to keep the wine exactly as the winemaker intended.

steps.prompt: Wines sealed with screw caps cannot suffer from cork taint.
steps.explanation: Yes. TCA, the cause of cork taint, comes from natural cork. Screw caps avoid it, although other faults are still possible.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fining, filtration and cold stabilisation make wine clear and stable
Corks let in a little oxygen but risk TCA
Screw caps keep wine fresh and avoid cork taint
